processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Bada: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one and carries the published price.
appearance_dry: As with other Bada large-leaf raw pu-erh, long dark olive leaves with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with Bada raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typically thick, large olive-green leaves, as with other Yunnan large-leaf tea.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about Zhanglang on its own. Bada tea as a whole is strong and bitter with a lasting sweet finish and plum and honey aromas.

brewing.notes: As with other Bada teas, start light and short, then lengthen once you know how firm the bitterness is.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored. Old-tree and younger arbor leaf sell at very different prices: one published spring list has old-tree at 1500 to 1600 yuan per kilo against 250 for arbor, so ask which it is.
description:
Zhanglang is a village on Bada Mountain in Xiding township, Menghai County, and a Bulang community with old tea trees. Bada runs from about 1,580 to 2,000 metres.

The leaf follows the usual raw pu-erh route, with sun-drying and no ripe-style piling.

Little is recorded about what sets Zhanglang apart in the cup. Bada in general is firm and bitter with a lasting sweetness and plum and honey in the aroma, so use that as a guide and adjust as you go.

When buying, the split that matters is old-tree against younger arbor leaf, as the price gap shows. Ask a seller which you are getting, and be wary of a cheap cake sold on the village name.
history:
Old Zhanglang is credited with a history of more than 1,400 years, with its tea trees said to have been planted by Bulang ancestors. That figure comes from the tea trade and local tradition and is not a documented date.

Today the village's name shows up on regional spring price lists as a Bada old-tree tea, a sign of how the single-village market has made it known.
